   503

    86	and obtains the metrics from either the resource metrics API (for per-pod resource metrics),
    87	or the custom metrics API (for all other metrics).
    88	
    89	- For per-pod resource metrics (like CPU), the controller fetches the metrics
    90	  from the resource metrics API for each Pod targeted by the HorizontalPodAutoscaler.
    91	  Then, if a target utilization value is set, the controller calculates the utilization
    92	  value as a percentage of the equivalent
    93	  [resource request](/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/#requests-and-limits)
    94	  on the containers in each Pod. If a target raw value is set, the raw metric values are used directly.
    95	  The controller then takes the mean of the utilization or the raw value (depending on the type
    96	  of target specified) across all targeted Pods, and produces a ratio used to scale
    97	  the number of desired replicas.

   100	  CPU utilization for the Pod will not be defined and the autoscaler will
   101	  not take any action for that metric. See the [algorithm details](#algorithm-details) section below
   102	  for more information about how the autoscaling algorithm works.
   103	
   104	- For per-pod custom metrics, the controller functions similarly to per-pod resource metrics,
   105	  except that it works with raw values, not utilization values.
   130	
   131	From the most basic perspective, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   132	operates on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric
   133	value:
   134	
   135	```math
   136	\begin{equation*}
   137	desiredReplicas = ceil\left\lceil currentReplicas \times \frac{currentMetricValue}{desiredMetricValue} \right\rceil
   138	\end{equation*}
   139	```
   140	
   141	For example, if the current metric value is `200m`, and the desired value
   142	is `100m`, the number of replicas will be doubled, since
   143	\\( { 200.0 \div 100.0 } = 2.0 \\).  
   144	If the current value is instead `50m`, you'll halve the number of
   145	replicas, since \\( { 50.0 \div 100.0 } = 0.5 \\). The control plane skips any scaling
   146	action if the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0 (within a globally-configurable
   147	tolerance, 0.1 by default).
   148	
   149	When a `targetAverageValue` or `targetAverageUtilization` is specified,
   150	the `currentMetricValue` is computed by taking the average of the given
   151	metric across all Pods in the HorizontalPodAutoscaler's scale target.
   152	
   153	Before checking the tolerance and deciding on the final values, the control
   154	plane also considers whether any metrics are missing, and how many Pods
   155	are [`Ready`](/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle/#pod-conditions).
   156	All Pods with a deletion timestamp set (objects with a deletion timestamp are
   157	in the process of being shut down / removed) are ignored, and all failed Pods
   158	are discarded.
   159	
   160	If a particular Pod is missing metrics, it is set aside for later; Pods
   161	with missing metrics will be used to adjust the final scaling amount.
   162	
   163	When scaling on CPU, if any pod has yet to become ready (it's still
   164	initializing, or possibly is unhealthy) _or_ the most recent metric point for
   165	the pod was before it became ready, that pod is set aside as well.
   166	
   167	Due to technical constraints, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler controller
   168	cannot exactly determine the first time a pod becomes ready when
   169	determining whether to set aside certain CPU metrics. Instead, it
   170	considers a Pod "not yet ready" if it's unready and transitioned to
   171	ready within a short, configurable window of time since it started.
   172	This value is configured with the `--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-initial-readiness-delay`
   173	flag, and its default is 30 seconds.
   174	Once a pod has become ready, it considers any transition to
   175	ready to be the first if it occurred within a longer, configurable time
   176	since it started. This value is configured with the
   177	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-cpu-initialization-period` flag, and its
   178	default is 5 minutes.
   179	
   180	The \\( currentMetricValue \over desiredMetricValue \\) base scale ratio is then
   181	calculated, using the remaining pods not set aside or discarded from above.
   182	
   183	If there were any missing metrics, the control plane recomputes the average more
   184	conservatively, assuming those pods were consuming 100% of the desired
   185	value in case of a scale down, and 0% in case of a scale up. This dampens
   186	the magnitude of any potential scale.
   187	
   188	Furthermore, if any not-yet-ready pods were present, and the workload would have
   189	scaled up without factoring in missing metrics or not-yet-ready pods,
   190	the controller conservatively assumes that the not-yet-ready pods are consuming 0%
   191	of the desired metric, further dampening the magnitude of a scale up.
   192	
   193	After factoring in the not-yet-ready pods and missing metrics, the
   194	controller recalculates the usage ratio. If the new ratio reverses the scale
   195	direction, or is within the tolerance, the controller doesn't take any scaling
   196	action. In other cases, the new ratio is used to decide any change to the
   197	number of Pods.
   198	
   199	Note that the _original_ value for the average utilization is reported
   200	back via the HorizontalPodAutoscaler status, without factoring in the
   201	not-yet-ready pods or missing metrics, even when the new usage ratio is
   202	used.
   203	
   204	If multiple metrics are specified in a HorizontalPodAutoscaler, this
   205	calculation is done for each metric, and then the largest of the desired
   206	replica counts is chosen. If any of these metrics cannot be converted
   207	into a desired replica count (e.g. due to an error fetching the metrics
   208	from the metrics APIs) and a scale down is suggested by the metrics which
   209	can be fetched, scaling is skipped. This means that the HPA is still capable
   210	of scaling up if one or more metrics give a `desiredReplicas` greater than
   211	the current value.
   212	
   213	Finally, right before HPA scales the target, the scale recommendation is recorded. The
   214	controller considers all recommendations within a configurable window choosing the
   215	highest recommendation from within that window. This value can be configured using the
   216	`--horizontal-pod-autoscaler-downscale-stabilization` flag, which defaults to 5 minutes.
   217	This means that scaledowns will occur gradually, smoothing out the impact of rapidly
   218	fluctuating metric values.

    95	
    96	Kubernetes offers features to help you run highly available applications even when you
    97	introduce frequent voluntary disruptions.
    98	
    99	As an application owner, you can create a PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) for each application.
   100	A PDB limits the number of Pods of a replicated application that are down simultaneously from
   101	voluntary disruptions. For example, a quorum-based application would
   102	like to ensure that the number of replicas running is never brought below the
   103	number needed for a quorum. A web front end might want to
   104	ensure that the number of replicas serving load never falls below a certain
   105	percentage of the total.
   106	
   107	Cluster managers and hosting providers should use tools which
   108	respect PodDisruptionBudgets by calling the [Eviction API](/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/safely-drain-node/#eviction-api)
   109	instead of directly deleting pods or deployments.
   110	
   111	For example, the `kubectl drain` subcommand lets you mark a node as going out of
   112	service. When you run `kubectl drain`, the tool tries to evict all of the Pods on
   113	the Node you're taking out of service. The eviction request that `kubectl` submits on
   114	your behalf may be temporarily rejected, so the tool periodically retries all failed
   115	requests until all Pods on the target node are terminated, or until a configurable timeout
   116	is reached.
   117	
   118	A PDB specifies the number of replicas that an application can tolerate having, relative to how
   119	many it is intended to have.  For example, a Deployment which has a `.spec.replicas: 5` is
   120	supposed to have 5 pods at any given time.  If its PDB allows for there to be 4 at a time,
   121	then the Eviction API will allow voluntary disruption of one (but not two) pods at a time.
   122	
   123	The group of pods that comprise the application is specified using a label selector, the same
   124	as the one used by the application's controller (deployment, stateful-set, etc).
   125	
   126	The "intended" number of pods is computed from the `.spec.replicas` of the workload resource
   127	that is managing those pods. The control plane discovers the owning workload resource by
   128	examining the `.metadata.ownerReferences` of the Pod.
   129	
   130	[Involuntary disruptions](#voluntary-and-involuntary-disruptions) cannot be prevented by PDBs; however they
   131	do count against the budget.
   132	
   133	Pods which are deleted or unavailable due to a rolling upgrade to an application do count
   134	against the disruption budget, but workload resources (such as Deployment and StatefulSet)
   135	are not limited by PDBs when doing rolling upgrades. Instead, the handling of failures
   136	during application updates is configured in the spec for the specific workload resource.
   137	
   138	It is recommended to set `AlwaysAllow` [Unhealthy Pod Eviction Policy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#unhealthy-pod-eviction-policy)
   139	to your PodDisruptionBudgets to support eviction of misbehaving applications during a node drain.
   140	The default behavior is to wait for the application pods to become [healthy](/docs/tasks/run-application/configure-pdb/#healthiness-of-a-pod)
   141	before the drain can proceed.

    27	## Requests and limits
    28	
    29	If the node where a Pod is running has enough of a resource available, it's possible (and

    32	For example, if you set a `memory` request of 256 MiB for a container, and that container is in

    42	
    43	`cpu` limits are enforced by CPU throttling. When a container approaches
    44	its `cpu` limit, the kernel will restrict access to the CPU corresponding to the
    45	container's limit. Thus, a `cpu` limit is a hard limit the kernel enforces.
    46	Containers may not use more CPU than is specified in their `cpu` limit.

    48	`memory` limits are enforced by the kernel with out of memory (OOM) kills. When
    49	a container uses more than its `memory` limit, the kernel may terminate it. However,
    50	terminations only happen when the kernel detects memory pressure. Thus, a
    51	container that over allocates memory may not be immediately killed. This means
    52	`memory` limits are enforced reactively. A container may use more memory than

   231	
   232	When you create a Pod, the Kubernetes scheduler selects a node for the Pod to
   233	run on. Each node has a maximum capacity for each of the resource types: the
   234	amount of CPU and memory it can provide for Pods. The scheduler ensures that,
   235	for each resource type, the sum of the resource requests of the scheduled
   236	containers is less than the capacity of the node.

   244

Decision: revise the design before production rollout. The proposed settings do not establish five available replicas through failures or updates, successful completion of long requests, or protection of database credentials and data. The recommendations below are configuration choices grounded in the supplied v1.32 documentation; their application-specific results require validation.

1. **PDB and rollout availability.** `minAvailable: 5` does not prevent node failure: involuntary disruptions cannot be prevented by PDBs, although they count against the budget. During a normal `kubectl drain`, eviction requests respect the PDB and can be rejected and retried; this protection depends on using the Eviction API rather than direct deletion. Deployment rolling updates are explicitly outside PDB enforcement. With six desired replicas, `maxUnavailable: 2` permits four available during an update. Recommend `maxUnavailable: 1, maxSurge: 1`, or conservatively `0/1` with sufficient spare capacity. These control rollout disruption, not simultaneous failures. Sources: [docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md, lines 99–141](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/disruptions.md#L99-L141); [docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md, lines 1183–1211](docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment.md#L1183-L1211).

2. **Zone placement.** Configure topology spread with an API-specific `labelSelector`, `topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone`, and `maxSkew: 1`, targeting two replicas per zone. `topologyKey` groups nodes by label value. With `DoNotSchedule`, skew limits the difference between the target domain’s matching-Pod count and the global minimum; violating placements remain unscheduled. `ScheduleAnyway` instead prefers lower skew while allowing placement. Choose explicitly between strict distribution and degraded-zone scheduling flexibility. An unavailable zone does not imply automatic successful redistribution: eligibility, taints, remaining capacity, and domain discovery matter. Setting `minDomains: 3` makes the global minimum zero when fewer than three eligible domains remain, potentially blocking replacements. Without it, the default is one. Removal also need not preserve balance. Sources: [docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md, lines 82–130, 179–189, 527–529, 605–623](docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/topology-spread-constraints.md#L82-L130).

3. **Probes for slow startup.** Use a startup probe with a failure budget sized to measured startup time. It disables readiness and liveness probes until startup succeeds; startup failure kills the container, with restart governed by restart policy. Then use readiness to indicate whether the API can serve requests, including required database availability. Failed readiness removes the Pod from matching Service endpoints without itself restarting the container. Use liveness for an unhealthy application that needs restarting, rather than making a database outage trigger restarts across the API fleet. Probe failures follow configured thresholds; endpoint removal is not documented as instantaneous completion or cancellation of existing requests. Sources: [docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md, lines 479–497, 512–556](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L479-L556); [docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md, lines 2176–2178](docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md#L2176-L2178).

4. **Termination and long requests.** The grace-period countdown starts **before** `preStop`. The kubelet runs that hook before asking the runtime to send TERM to the container’s main process; hook time therefore consumes the shutdown budget. An overrun can receive a one-off two-second extension. At grace expiry, remaining processes receive `SIGKILL`. Concurrently, terminating endpoints remain represented in EndpointSlices with `terminating` status and `ready: false`; `serving` supports draining decisions. Thirty seconds is a default/configuration value, not a guarantee requests finish. Implement signal handling and draining, then size grace time for hooks and measured request completion. Sources: [docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md, lines 1006–1008](docs/reference/kubernetes-api/workload-resources/pod-v1.md#L1006-L1008); [docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md, lines 591–639](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L591-L639).

5. **Resource requests and limits.** CPU requests influence scheduling capacity and, on Linux, CPU weighting under contention; they are not CPU ceilings. Containers can exceed requests when resources permit. CPU limits impose throttling, whereas memory limits are enforced reactively through OOM killing, potentially causing restarts. Set requests from workload measurements and test limits against latency and memory peaks. CPU-utilization HPA divides usage by requests: if relevant container requests are missing, Pod utilization is undefined and HPA takes no action for that metric. Inspect effective configuration because a limit can become the request when neither an explicit request nor admission default exists. Sources: [docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md, lines 29–66, 230–265](docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#L29-L66); [docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md, lines 89–102](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L89-L102).

6. **HPA damping and stabilization.** The basic recommendation is the ceiling of current replicas multiplied by current/desired metric value. HPA sets aside missing metrics and qualifying not-yet-ready CPU samples. Missing metrics are conservatively assumed at 100% of target for downscale and 0% for upscale; not-yet-ready Pods further dampen upscale using 0%. If recalculation reverses direction or falls within tolerance, scaling stops. Default tolerance is 10%; readiness handling uses configurable defaults of 30 seconds and a five-minute CPU initialization period. Default downscale stabilization chooses the highest recommendation within five minutes. Consequently, displayed utilization and the raw ratio need not predict actual scaling. A working metrics API is a prerequisite. Sources: [docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md, lines 113–116, 130–218](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L130-L218).

7. **Least-privilege networking.** Establish default-deny ingress and egress, then allow approved callers to the API port, API egress to the database port, and corresponding database ingress. Isolation applies independently in each direction. Policies combine additively: an existing allow-all policy defeats narrower restrictions. Both source egress and destination ingress must permit a connection; reply traffic is implicitly allowed. Preserve DNS egress to the actual cluster resolver, including the documented UDP/TCP 53 service pattern, and validate cluster-specific addressing. Supporting CNI/network-policy enforcement is mandatory: merely creating policy objects has no effect without an implementing controller. Sources: [docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md, lines 45–81, 234–259](docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies.md#L45-L81); [docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md, lines 158–174](docs/tasks/administer-cluster/dns-debugging-resolution.md#L158-L174).

8. **Secrets protection.** Base64 is serialization, not adequate confidentiality; the docs explicitly describe encoded credentials as obscured but not secret. Reject encoded production credentials in Git. Enable encryption at rest and least-privilege RBAC, and expose credentials only to containers requiring them. Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd by default. Restricting direct Secret reads alone is insufficient: permission to create Pods—including indirectly through Deployments—allows reading namespace Secrets through those workloads. Review workload-creation permissions alongside Secret access. Encryption at rest does not establish protection for repository copies. Sources: [docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/secret-v1.md, lines 45–47](docs/reference/kubernetes-api/config-and-storage-resources/secret-v1.md#L45-L47); [docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md, lines 35–48, 305–307](docs/concepts/configuration/secret.md#L35-L48).

9. **Storage lifecycle.** Changing a StorageClass reclaim policy does not retroactively update existing PVs; inspect and patch those PVs individually. Dynamically provisioned PVs inherit the class policy, defaulting to `Delete`. After PVC deletion, `Retain` preserves the released PV and data for manual reclamation; supported `Delete` removes both PV and backing storage. StatefulSet deletion/scaling is a separate trigger: PVCs default to retention. Optional `whenDeleted` and `whenScaled` policies can delete template-created PVCs after affected Pods disappear, subject to the documented feature prerequisite. Those PVC deletions then expose the PV reclaim behavior. Sources: [docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md, lines 126–135](docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes.md#L126-L135); [docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md, lines 178–210](docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#L178-L210); [docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md, lines 391–423](docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset.md#L391-L423).

10. **Prioritized rollout and validation.** First remove Git-held credentials, verify encryption/RBAC, and audit existing PV reclaim settings and database PVC retention. Next implement probes, draining, resource requests, compatible rollout settings, and explicit zone constraints. Apply tested network restrictions with DNS allowances. Finally exercise rollout, drain, node/zone loss, startup spikes, missing metrics, and storage recovery. Validate at least four unresolved limits: actual request-drain duration, remaining-zone capacity, CPU utilization’s relationship to API latency, and database recovery/data durability. The documents establish mechanisms, not those application outcomes. Sources: [pod lifecycle, lines 619–639](docs/concepts/workloads/pods/pod-lifecycle.md#L619-L639); [resource scheduling, lines 230–241](docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers.md#L230-L241); [HPA, lines 183–218](docs/tasks/run-application/horizontal-pod-autoscale.md#L183-L218); [PV reclamation, lines 178–210](docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes.md#L178-L210).
